text: Everything so far predicted a number. Many real questions ask for a category instead — will this customer churn, is this transaction fraud. Logistic regression is the classic tool for predicting a yes-or-no outcome. Despite the word regression in its name, it's actually a classification model, and the natural bridge from the linear models of this chapter to the classifiers ahead.

Suppose churn is coded 1 for left and 0 for stayed. A straight line predicting that target will happily output 1.4 or negative 0.3 — not probabilities at all. Logistic regression fixes this by feeding the usual linear score through the sigmoid function, which squashes any number into the range 0 to 1. A large positive score gives a probability near 1, a large negative score near 0, and a score of exactly 0 gives 0.5.

Simulating 400 customers where longer tenure means lower churn risk, fitting LogisticRegression gives an intercept of 2.35 and a coefficient of negative 0.107 — close to the built-in truth of 2.0 and negative 0.09. One thing to know: scikit-learn's LogisticRegression applies L2 regularization by default, the ridge idea from last lesson, which is part of why the fitted values differ slightly from the truth.

predict_proba returns two columns — the probability of not churning, then of churning. A 6-month customer has an 85 percent churn probability; a 36-month customer has just 18 percent. predict applies a threshold of 0.5 by default, so the first customer is labeled true, will churn, and the second false.

You can pick a different threshold — lower it to catch more churners at the cost of more false alarms. Accuracy on the test set is 0.79. The confusion matrix breaks that down — of 61 customers who stayed, 52 were right and 9 were flagged as churners; of 39 who churned, 27 were caught and 12 were missed.
Plotting the dots as actual outcomes and the crimson S-curve as predicted probability shows exactly where the model crosses the 0.5 threshold — right around 22 months of tenure.

A coefficient in logistic regression acts on the log-odds. Exponentiating it gives an odds ratio — e to the negative 0.107 is about 0.90. Each additional month of tenure multiplies a customer's odds of churning by about 0.90, roughly a 10 percent reduction in the odds, holding other features fixed. That's a change in odds, not directly in probability.

A few things to remember. Like linear regression, the model draws a straight boundary in feature space, so it struggles with tangled, non-linear patterns unless you add engineered features. Scale features when using regularization, just like the previous lesson. And with imbalanced classes, accuracy can mislead — always check the confusion matrix and consider the threshold.

To recap: logistic regression passes a linear score through the sigmoid to get a probability, then applies a threshold to make a decision. It's fast, interpretable through odds ratios, and a strong baseline for any yes-or-no problem. Next, we look at a very different family of models: decision trees.
